titre: An Island That Discovery Alone Failed to Keep
accroche: In 1906, an American general finds a Dutch flag on an island the United States believed was theirs. An arbitrator will rule twenty-two years later.
contenu_vulgarise:
In January 1906, American General Leonard Wood inspects Miangas, an islet of just over three square kilometers (about 1.2 square miles) between the Philippines and Celebes. The Philippines have just come under American sovereignty, ceded by Spain in 1898 by the Treaty of Paris. Wood expects to find American territory. Instead he finds a Dutch flag, planted by the colonial administration of the East Indies.

The disagreement drags on for nearly twenty years before Washington and The Hague agree, in 1925, to submit it to a single arbitrator appointed by the Permanent Court of Arbitration: the Swiss jurist Max Huber. He delivers his award on April 4, 1928.

## Continuous Presence Outweighs a Single Act

The United States relies on the cession from Spain, which itself claimed sovereignty over the island from its discovery in the sixteenth century and from a 1648 treaty with the United Provinces. The Netherlands answers with the history of their actual presence: since the early eighteenth century, the Dutch East India Company and then the colonial administration had formed ties of allegiance with the local chiefs, collected tribute, and enforced their authority, without any other power ever contesting it on the ground.

Huber rules in favor of the Netherlands. His central formula comes down to one simple idea: discovery alone creates only an incomplete title. To become sovereignty enforceable against other states, it must be completed by the real and continuous exercise of authority, something the law of the time already required but that Spain, absorbed elsewhere in the archipelago, had never done on this particular spot. Huber adds a principle that goes beyond the dispute itself, that of intertemporal law: the creation of a right is judged in light of the law in force when the act that founds it was performed, but its continued existence must follow the conditions set by later developments in the law.

## What a Planted Flag Can Never Prove

The Palmas award has since become one of the most cited precedents in any territorial dispute that pits an old founding act against a more recent real administration.

What Palmas shifts is the idea that a solemn act, however old and well documented, would amount to sovereignty by itself. A planted flag, an expedition recorded in a treaty, a name given on a map are only the beginnings of proof. What international law looks at is what happened next, year after year, on the very ground one claims to govern.

citation.texte: The continuous and peaceful display of territorial sovereignty (peaceful in relation to other States) is as good as a title.
citation.source: Island of Palmas (Netherlands v. United States), arbitral award of April 4, 1928, Reports of International Arbitral Awards, vol. II, p. 839

carte.punch: A planted flag proves nothing. What counts is what happened next, over time.
carte.idee: In 1928, arbitrator Max Huber settles a twenty-year-old dispute between the Netherlands and the United States over a Pacific island. His award sets a rule still cited today: discovery creates only an incomplete title, and only authority exercised without interruption makes sovereignty.

quiz.question: According to Max Huber's 1928 award, why does Dutch sovereignty prevail over the American claim based on Spanish discovery?
choix: Because a vote held among the island's inhabitants confirmed their preference for the Dutch East Indies
Because the Netherlands had defeated Spain in a naval conflict specifically over this island
Because Spanish discovery was only an incomplete title, completed on the Dutch side by authority exercised without interruption
Because the 1898 Treaty of Paris explicitly excluded Miangas from the cession to Washington
quiz.explication: Huber writes that discovery creates only an incomplete title: for it to become sovereignty enforceable against others, there had to be a real and continuous exercise of authority. It is that continuity, supplied by the Dutch colonial administration and absent on the Spanish and then American side, that decides the case, not a treaty or an armed conflict.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what did Spain base its claim to sovereignty over Miangas, later ceded to the United States?
choix: On its discovery of the island in the sixteenth century and a 1648 treaty with the United Provinces
On continuous military occupation since the early eighteenth century
On tribute paid every year by the island's local chiefs
On a decision of the Permanent Court of Arbitration handed down in 1906
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text reports that Spain claimed sovereignty from its discovery of the island in the sixteenth century, backed by a 1648 treaty concluded with the United Provinces.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the principle of intertemporal law set out by Max Huber add to his decision?
choix: Treaties signed before 1900 are automatically void before an international tribunal
The creation of a right is judged by the law of its time, but its continued existence must follow the conditions set by later developments in the law
Only the law in force at the time of judgment matters, whatever the date of the facts
A territorial title must be formally renewed every fifty years to remain valid
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Huber distinguishes the creation of a right, judged by the law in force when the founding act was performed, from its continued existence, which must follow the conditions set by later developments in the law.

quiz_supplementaire.question: By which treaty do the Philippines come under American sovereignty, opening the way for Washington's claim to Miangas?
choix: The Treaty of Münster, signed in 1648 between Spain and the United Provinces
The Treaty of Paris, signed on December 10, 1898 between Spain and the United States
The special agreement of January 23, 1925 between The Hague and Washington
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Treaty of Paris of December 10, 1898 cedes the Philippines from Spain to the United States; Washington considers that this cession includes Miangas, which the Netherlands disputes.
